### Available skills
- imagegen: Generate or edit raster images when the task benefits from AI-created bitmap visuals such as photos, illustrations, textures, sprites, mockups, or transparent-background cutouts. Use when Codex should create a brand-new image, transform an existing image, or derive visual variants from references, and the output should be a bitmap asset rather than repo-native code or vector. Do not use when the task is better handled by editing existing SVG/vector/code-native assets, extending an established icon or logo system, or building the visual directly in HTML/CSS/canvas. (file: r0/imagegen/SKILL.md)
- openai-docs: Use for Codex models/pricing, scheduled tasks, skills, settings, setup, troubleshooting, customization, automations, and self-knowledge—including 'you,' 'your,' 'this app,' or 'this coding agent' when they refer to Codex—and for OpenAI APIs/products and ChatGPT Work. Also use for model choice/migration, prompting, SDKs, Responses, Realtime, agents, evals, and Chat/Work/Codex comparisons. Do not use for generic app/software tasks that merely mention Codex. (file: r0/openai-docs/SKILL.md)
- plugin-creator: Create and scaffold plugin directories for Codex with a required `.codex-plugin/plugin.json`, optional plugin folders/files, valid manifest defaults, and personal-marketplace entries by default. Use when Codex needs to create a new personal plugin, add optional plugin structure, generate or update marketplace entries for plugin ordering and availability metadata, or update an existing local plugin during development with the CLI-driven cachebuster and reinstall flow. (file: r0/plugin-creator/SKILL.md)
- skill-creator: Create or update a Codex skill with appropriately scoped instructions and any needed supporting resources. (file: r0/skill-creator/SKILL.md)
- skill-installer: Install Codex skills into $CODEX_HOME/skills from a curated list or a GitHub repo path. Use when a user asks to list installable skills, install a curated skill, or install a skill from another repo (including private repos). (file: r0/skill-installer/SKILL.md)
- browser:control-in-app-browser: Control the in-app Browser for opening, navigating, inspecting visible or interactive page state, clicking, typing, screenshots, and local web testing. It can have existing signed-in sessions. For semantic operations on linked resources, prefer a purpose-built connector, API, or CLI when available. (file: r1/browser/26.825.41651/skills/control-in-app-browser/SKILL.md)
- chrome:control-chrome: Control the user's Chrome browser for tasks that depend on existing Chrome state: tabs, logged-in sessions, or extensions. Prefer purpose-built connectors, APIs, or CLIs when available. (file: r1/chrome/26.825.41651/skills/control-chrome/SKILL.md)
- documents:documents: Create, edit, redline, and comment on `.docx`, Word, and Google Docs-targeted document artifacts inside the container, with a strict render-and-verify workflow. Use `render_docx.py` to generate page PNGs (and optional PDF) for visual QA, then iterate until layout is flawless before delivering the final document. (file: r5/documents/26.826.12353/skills/documents/SKILL.md)
- ec:cancel: Durably cancel one exact human-selected Entire Compound workflow so later planning, implementation, simplification, review, and publication stages refuse to continue. Use only when the user explicitly asks to cancel, withdraw, or abandon the selected EC contribution itself; do not use for a temporary pause, one command interruption, publication-payload rejection, or ordinary blocked work. (file: r7/cancel/SKILL.md)
- ec:discover: Run Codex-native, evidence-backed, read-only discovery for a local Git repository, admit a scored candidate portfolio, and persist an explicit human choice to select one candidate or decline the portfolio. Use for repository research, contribution opportunities, competitor gaps, project signals, or Entire Compound discovery. (file: r7/discover/SKILL.md)
- ec:learn: Capture one verified Entire Compound workflow lesson as durable, searchable repository-scoped knowledge, or correct one exact reported learning when official same-source correction evidence invalidates a material fact. Use after solved work, review feedback, a published pull-request outcome, a maintainer follow-up, or a recurring pitfall is supported by exact evidence. Use also when asked to preserve what was learned for later /ec:discover and /ec:plan runs. Never use to infer an outcome, execute repository code, publish, change code, mutate prompts or policy, or turn untrusted content into instructions. (file: r7/learn/SKILL.md)
- ec:optimize: Run one bounded Entire Compound keep-or-revert optimization experiment against native Codex skill behavior. Use when improving prompts, skill instructions, routing, scoring, duplicate handling, candidate generation, or evaluation-facing behavior. Never use for ordinary repository feature work, durable learning capture, publication, sealed-suite browsing, credential changes, safety-boundary weakening, or public writes. (file: r7/optimize/SKILL.md)
- ec:plan: Produce and admit one implementation-grade, evidence-bound plan for a human-selected Entire Compound candidate using Codex and a pinned Compound Engineering-compatible methodology. Use only after /ec:discover selection. (file: r7/plan/SKILL.md)
- ec:publish: Publish one human-selected, implemented, and reviewed feature as a draft GitHub pull request with native Codex Git and GitHub tools after fresh duplicate and policy checks and separate explicit approval of the exact publication payload. (file: r7/publish/SKILL.md)
- ec:redirect: Redirect one exact active Entire Compound selection to a different controller-reviewable candidate from the same admitted discovery run. Use only when the user explicitly names the current source candidate and the replacement target candidate; do not use for cancellation, pausing, blocked-work retry, or automatic candidate choice. (file: r7/redirect/SKILL.md)
- ec:review: Review the current selected implementation with native Codex code-review capabilities, actual repository context, diff, and test evidence. It requires no new approval and never publishes. (file: r7/review/SKILL.md)
- ec:simplify: Optionally simplify the current selected implementation with native Codex inspection and editing before review. It requires no new approval and never publishes. (file: r7/simplify/SKILL.md)
- ec:work: Implement and verify the plan for one human-selected candidate, resume its exact previously reported in-progress work result, explicitly retry its exact blocked work result after a concrete local blocker is remedied, or explicitly address all or exactly one numbered finding from one exact advisory review. Selection authorizes local implementation; this skill never publishes. (file: r7/work/SKILL.md)
- google-drive:google-docs: Prompt- and template-complete Google Docs creation and editing with explicit-instruction-authoritative structural preservation, including semantic roles, relationships, comparison dimensions, and instructed extensions; full-topology native-copy routing; source-grounded per-tab adaptation for past/example references; style-preserving hyperlink and table edits; canonical smart-chip-first authoring for dates and relevant supported people or Google resources; a file-backed advisory trusted read before existing-document writes; automatic protected-control awareness; direct connector APIs by default; DOCX-first import only when no supplied Google Doc template/reference constrains the output; and checked-in code mode only for exact native dropdown mutation. Use when Codex must create, edit, fill, adapt, redesign, or verify Google Docs without overriding explicit user/template instructions, adding unrequested document scope, or carrying stale reference facts into a new deliverable. (file: r3/google-docs/SKILL.md)
- google-drive:google-drive: Use connected Google Drive as the single entrypoint for Drive, Docs, Sheets, and Slides work. Use when the user wants to find, fetch, organize, share, export, copy, or delete Drive files, or summarize and edit Google Docs, Google Sheets, and Google Slides through one unified Google Drive plugin. (file: r3/google-drive/SKILL.md)
- google-drive:google-drive-comments: Write, reply to, and resolve Google Drive comments on Docs, Sheets, Slides, and Drive files with evidence-backed location context. Use when the user asks to leave comments, review a file with comments, respond to comment threads, or resolve Drive comments. (file: r3/google-drive-comments/SKILL.md)
- google-drive:google-sheets: Analyze and edit connected Google Sheets with range precision. Use when the user wants to create Google Sheets, find a spreadsheet, inspect tabs or ranges, search rows, plan formulas, create or repair charts, clean or restructure tables, write concise summaries, or make explicit cell-range updates. (file: r3/google-sheets/SKILL.md)
- google-drive:google-slides: Route Google Slides authoring requests and derive a design system from a native template or reference deck. Use this skill when the user provides an existing native Google Slides deck as a template, reference, or prior-period source, or asks to edit, update, repair, restyle, or clean up an existing native Google Slides deck. Use the Presentations skill instead for net-new presentation creation when no existing native Google Slides deck must be followed. (file: r3/google-slides/SKILL.md)
- pdf:pdf: Read, create, inspect, render, and verify PDF files where visual layout matters, including fillable AcroForms. Use Poppler rendering plus Python tools such as reportlab, pdfplumber, and pypdf for generation and extraction. (file: r5/pdf/26.826.12353/skills/pdf/SKILL.md)
- plugin-management:plugin-management: Discover and suggest relevant plugins, inspect app permissions and dependencies, and manage plugin connections or removal. Use when the user asks about plugins or when a task would materially benefit from an external app, account, service, or data source that available tools cannot access. (file: r4/plugin-management/0.1.0/skills/plugin-management/SKILL.md)
- presentations:Presentations: Read, create or edit PowerPoint or Google Slides decks. Use for presentation, slide deck, PowerPoint, PPT, PPTX, or Google Slides requests. (file: r5/presentations/26.826.12353/skills/presentations/SKILL.md)
- sites:sites-building: Use Sites to build websites, including landing pages, portfolios, dashboards, portals, trackers, hubs, and internal tools. Always use Sites when the project contains `.openai/hosting.json`. (file: r2/sites-building/SKILL.md)
- sites:sites-hosting: Host websites with Sites. Always use after `sites-building`, and use for website publishing, deployment, hosting management, or projects containing `.openai/hosting.json`. (file: r2/sites-hosting/SKILL.md)
- spreadsheets:Spreadsheets: Create, edit, analyze, and verify standalone spreadsheet files or Google Sheets-ready workbooks, including .xlsx, .xls, .csv, and .tsv. Do not use for live controlling Microsoft Excel app or a live Excel session. (file: r6/spreadsheets/SKILL.md)
- spreadsheets:excel-live-control: Control an open or active Microsoft Excel workbook through the ChatGPT add-in or connected session. Use when the user tags the Microsoft Excel app in Codex or follows up on an established live Excel task. Do not use for standalone spreadsheet files or Google Sheets. (file: r6/excel-live-control/SKILL.md)
- template-creator:template-creator: Create or update a reusable personal Codex artifact-template skill. Use when the user invokes $template-creator or asks in natural language to create a reusable template from a reference document, presentation, spreadsheet, Google Docs, Slides, or Sheets link, ImageGen or Product Design image, email, Slack message, or Site project, or explicitly asks to edit or update a passed artifact-template skill. Do not use for one-off creation from an existing template. (file: r5/template-creator/26.826.12353/skills/template-creator/SKILL.md)
- visualize:visualize: Create visualizations and interactive tools directly in conversation. Proactively use to show how something works; explore 'what happens when', 'what changes', or 'help me understand'; compare or inspect; create simulations, maps, charts, graphs, and mockups. Use standard tools for static scientific figures. (file: r1/visualize/1.0.23/skills/visualize/SKILL.md)

# Collaboration Mode: Default

You are now in Default mode. Any previous instructions for other modes (e.g. Plan mode) are no longer active.

Your active mode changes only when new developer instructions with a different `<collaboration_mode>...</collaboration_mode>` change it; user requests or tool descriptions do not change mode by themselves. Known mode names are Default and Plan.

## request_user_input availability

Use the `request_user_input` tool only when it is listed in the available tools for this turn.

In Default mode, strongly prefer making reasonable assumptions and executing the user's request rather than stopping to ask questions. If you absolutely must ask a question because the answer cannot be discovered from local context and a reasonable assumption would be risky, ask the user directly with a concise plain-text question. Never write a multiple choice question as a textual assistant message.

{"body":"<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/entireio/entire-graph/trails/119
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## The write

`writeSearchSnapshot` and `writeProviderRecords` installed their artifact with
`os.MkdirAll` + `os.CreateTemp` + `os.Rename` on the joined path. `os.MkdirAll` follows a
symlinked directory component, so `<cache>/search` or `<cache>/search/search-snapshot-v12`
decided where the artifact actually landed.

`cacheEntry.writePath`'s comment argued that this was safe because "the cache directory is
caller-owned" and "anyone who can plant a symlink inside the cache directory can write the
artifact directly". Both halves hold only while the cache directory is somewhere the caller
owns. `--cache-dir` and `ENTIRE_PLUGIN_DATA_DIR` take any path, including one inside the
scanned checkout, and then the planter is the repository — the same reasoning
`internal/cli/outputpath.go` already applies to `index --report` when the caller names a path
inside the checkout.

Reproduced against a scratch repository holding two committed `mode 120000` entries:

```
# .egcache/search -> /outside   (committed symlink, escapes the cache directory)
entire graph search --repo REPO --head --query q --cache-dir REPO/.egcache
  -> /outside/search-snapshot-v12/<sha256>.json.gz

# .git-linked family, cache directory at the checkout root
#   search -> .git   (committed symlink, stays inside the opened root)
entire graph search --repo REPO --head --query q --cache-dir REPO
  -> REPO/.git/search-snapshot-v12/<sha256>.json.gz
```

The destination filename is a digest, so this creates directories and files rather than
overwriting a chosen victim, and `os.Rename` already replaced a symlink at the artifact name
instead of following it. The directory components were the whole of the hole.

## The same defect is also a permanent cache miss

`cacheEntry.open` reads through `os.OpenRoot(cacheDir)`, which refuses exactly the components
the write followed — `TestCacheEntryReadRejectsSymlinkEscape` pins that. So a symlinked
descendant produced an entry that was **written on every run and read on none**. Measured on
the same repository and query, artifact mtime after two runs:

```
plain cache directory:      1787885558, 1787885558   (hit, not rewritten)
symlinked family component: 1787885508, 1787885561   (miss, rewritten every run)
```

That is why the refusal costs nothing that works today: every configuration it now rejects has
never produced a cache hit.

## The fix

`cacheEntry.write` replaces both bodies. The cache root stays caller-named and is still
resolved as given, so a symlinked cache *directory* — the deployment that puts the cache on
another volume, in a shared location, or outside a container's writable layer — keeps working
on both sides. Below the root, each component is created and then `Lstat`-checked before being
descended into through its own opened handle, and a symlink there is refused.

`os.Root` alone is not enough for the second half, for the reason `outputpath.go` records: it
stops a link leaving the root but follows one that stays inside it, and with the cache
directory at a checkout root, `.git` is inside it. The `Lstat` check is not an exact-case
comparison, so a case-insensitive filesystem cannot answer it with a differently-spelled link.

The temporary file moves with it: a `crypto/rand` name opened `O_CREATE|O_EXCL` inside the
checked directory handle, keeping the `.snapshot-*.json.gz` / `.records-*.json.gz` shape that
cleanup globs match, and the install is `Rename` within that same handle.

Query-time caching is best effort and those call sites discard the error, so a refusal is a
cache miss there. `index`'s explicit persist reports it:

```
persist preindex snapshot: cache directory component "search" is a symlink
```

## Tests

`internal/sem/cache_write_confinement_test.go`, all five refusal assertions verified to fail
with the production change reverted and the tests kept:

- family component symlinked out of the cache directory (both families)
- family component symlinked to `.git`, staying inside the opened root (both families)
- version component symlinked out

plus three that pin what must not change: a symlinked cache root still round-trips at mode
0600, a symlink at the artifact name is replaced rather than written through, and a successful
write leaves only the artifact.

## Two existing tests changed, and why

`TestCacheWritesTolerateSymlinkedCacheDirectories` pinned the old behaviour, calling a symlinked
family subdirectory "a supported operator layout (a larger volume, a shared cache, an escape from
a container's writable layer)" whose artifact "must still be written **and read back through it**".

The read-back half was never true, and nothing asserted it. Every one of those three motivations
needs a link that LEAVES the cache directory, and that is exactly what the reader refuses.
Measured on unmodified `main`, with `cache/search -> ../backing`:

```
write:     ok, artifact lands in backing/v1/<key>.json.gz
read back: openat search/v1/<key>.json.gz: path escapes from parent
```

The only family link that does round-trip is one pointing back inside the cache directory, which
cannot reach another volume. So the test is replaced by
`TestCacheWritesRefuseSymlinkedFamilyDirectories`, which pins both halves: an artifact placed
behind the link by hand is still unreachable through it, and the write no longer pretends
otherwise.

`TestSearchCacheLoadersRejectSymlinkEscape`'s last block asserted that `preindex` persists beneath
such a cache directory. It now asserts the refusal and that the message names the component: an
entry the durability read cannot see is not a durable artifact, so reporting it is the honest
outcome for a verb whose whole job is to promise one.

## Verification

`go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, `gofmt -l` clean, and `go test ./...` green across every package
(`internal/sem` 863s, `internal/cli` 153s under load).

CI is green on all three platforms, including the Windows mode-bits fix in the second commit.

Correction to an earlier claim in this description: one test was skipped in the local run above,
`TestWriteOutputFileDoesNotFollowALinkSwappedInAfterTheCheck`
(`internal/cli/outputpath_test.go`), because it blew a 4-minute timeout locally — including on an
unmodified `origin/main` worktree, which is why it was reported as unrelated to this change. CI has
since run it on all three platforms and it passes, so it was local starvation (the test spins until
it wins a race, and this machine was running several suites concurrently), not a non-termination.
Nothing is outstanding against it.

Every claim above was reproduced by driving the built binary against a scratch repository with
committed `mode 120000` entries, before and after, for both cache families.

","comments":[{"author":"suhaanthayyil","body":"Adversarial re-review. The `writePath` migration is complete and the write-side component walk does what it says. But the central regression argument is wrong for in-root links, and the read side was not brought along.

**1. BREAKS a layout that works today.** The PR justifies breaking symlinked family/version components with: "reads go through `os.OpenRoot(cacheDir)`, which refuses exactly that — so the artifact was written on every run and read on none." That holds only for links that *leave* the cache directory. `os.Root` **follows** an in-root link. `cacheEntry.open()` on this branch is unchanged and is still `root.Open(entry.relative)` — so `<cache>/search -> <cache>/bigstore` (a shared or relocated family directory that stays under the root) read *and* wrote fine on `main`, and after this PR `entire graph index` hard-fails on it. `search_cache_test.go`'s hunk converting `preindexProviderSnapshotWithPersistenceReader` from success to a hard error is the same shape of change. Head is now `30d490af`.

---

### 1. `internal/sem/cache_entry.go:183` — Windows junctions are `ModeIrregular`, not `ModeSymlink` — **VALID**

The guard tested `info.Mode()&fs.ModeSymlink != 0`. That is the right test on Unix and the wrong one on Windows: a symlink is reported as `ModeSymlink`, but a directory junction or mount point is reported as `ModeIrregular`. A junction planted at the `family` or `version` component therefore passed the check and was then descended into and followed — exactly the redirect this guard exists to refuse.

This repository already had the correct predicate, with five production call sites:

```
internal/sem/path_redirect_windows.go:12   return info.Mode()&(os.ModeSymlink|os.ModeIrregular) != 0
internal/sem/path_redirect_other.go:8      return info.Mode()&os.ModeSymlink != 0
```
callers: `provider.go:11777`, `provider.go:13200`, `provider.go:15057`, `sweep_open_other.go:68`, `metadata_tree_entry_windows.go:37` — all in `package sem`, so it is a drop-in here.

**Fix:** `openCacheComponent` now calls `cacheComponentRedirectError`, which tests `pathMayRedirect(info)`. The message keeps the substring `is a symlink` that `search_cache_test.go:161` matches on, and names the mode it found.

---

### 2. `internal/sem/cache_entry.go:194` — `rand.Text()` terminates the process — **VALID** (and stronger than described)

Verified in the toolchain's own source. `crypto/rand.Text` calls `Read`, and `crypto/rand/rand.go`:

```go
// Read calls [io.ReadFull] on [Reader] and crashes the program irrecoverably if
// an error is returned. …
	if err != nil {
		fatal("crypto/rand: failed to read random data (see https://go.dev/issue/66821): " + err.Error())
		panic("unreachable") // To be sure.
	}
```

`fatal` is `runtime.fatal` via `go:linkname`, reaching `fatalthrow` — the runtime's unrecoverable throw. So it is **not** a panic a caller can `recover`; it is a hard process kill. Tearing down a whole index run because a temporary cache file could not be named is the wrong failure mode for a best-effort write whose errors every caller already discards.

For contrast, `os.CreateTemp` never has this exposure: `$GOROOT/src/os/tempfile.go` names its files from `runtime.rand()`, an infallible non-cryptographic source. This code wants the CSPRNG for the O_EXCL race guard, so the answer is not to drop to a weaker source but to read it through an interface that reports.

**Fix:** `cacheTempNameSuffix(source io.Reader)` reads 16 bytes with `io.ReadFull(rand.Reader, …)` and hex-encodes them — same CSPRNG, error returned instead of a process kill.

---

### 3. `internal/sem/cache_entry.go:186` — TOCTOU between `Lstat` and `OpenRoot` — **REFUTED**

The race window is real; the consequence it implies is not. `os.Root` enforces confinement inside the syscall, independently of any `Lstat` the caller did first, so winning the race cannot make the write escape the cache root.

Standalone probe against the same toolchain (`go1.26.0 darwin/arm64`), exercising every operation this code performs through the returned handle:

```
A OpenRoot(link -> ../outside RELATIVE): ERROR: openat link: path escapes from parent
B OpenRoot(link -> ABS outside path):    ERROR: openat link: path escapes from parent
C OpenRoot(link -> sibling INSIDE root): OK (no error)
C sub.Open(in.txt):                      SUCCESS, read "INSIDE-BYTES"
D OpenFile(link/x -> ../outside REL):    ERROR: openat link/x: path escapes from parent
E OpenFile(link/y -> ABS outside path):  ERROR: openat link/y: path escapes from parent
F Rename(src.txt -> link/z.txt):         ERROR: renameat src.txt link/z.txt: path escapes from parent
```

`go doc os.Root`:

> Methods on Root will follow symbolic links, but symbolic links may not reference a location outside the root. Symbolic links must not be absolute.

So the worst a won race can do is case C: redirect the write to **another location inside the same cache root**, which `os.Root` permits by design. That is not a privilege gain — whoever can plant the symlink at that component already has write access to the cache directory and can simply write the target path directly. The `Lstat` is a nicer error ahead of an enforcement that happens anyway, not the boundary itself.

No change made. Closing the window would mean re-deriving through a handle `os.Root` already re-derives, for an outcome `os.Root` already guarantees.

(The one documented exception is `GOOS=js`, where `os.Root` states it *is* vulnerable to symlink TOCTOU and cannot ensure confinement. This tool is not built for js/wasm.)

---

### Tests

In `internal/sem/cache_write_confinement_test.go`:

- `TestCacheComponentRedirectErrorHonoursEveryRedirectingMode` — table over `ModeDir`, `ModeSymlink`, `ModeIrregular|ModeDir`, presented through a stub `os.FileInfo`. - `TestCacheTempNameSuffixIsUnpredictable` — 64 distinct 32-character lowercase-hex draws.
- `TestCreateRootTempNamesTheFileFromTheReportedRandomSource` — the call-site guard; the hex shape is what distinguishes it from `rand.Text`.

## The write

`writeSearchSnapshot` and `writeProviderRecords` installed their artifact with
`os.MkdirAll` + `os.CreateTemp` + `os.Rename` on the joined path. `os.MkdirAll` follows a
symlinked directory component, so `<cache>/search` or `<cache>/search/search-snapshot-v12`
decided where the artifact actually landed.

`cacheEntry.writePath`'s comment argued that this was safe because "the cache directory is
caller-owned" and "anyone who can plant a symlink inside the cache directory can write the
artifact directly". Both halves hold only while the cache directory is somewhere the caller
owns. `--cache-dir` and `ENTIRE_PLUGIN_DATA_DIR` take any path, including one inside the
scanned checkout, and then the planter is the repository — the same reasoning
`internal/cli/outputpath.go` already applies to `index --report` when the caller names a path
inside the checkout.

Reproduced against a scratch repository holding two committed `mode 120000` entries:

```
# .egcache/search -> /outside   (committed symlink, escapes the cache directory)
entire graph search --repo REPO --head --query q --cache-dir REPO/.egcache
  -> /outside/search-snapshot-v12/<sha256>.json.gz

# .git-linked family, cache directory at the checkout root
#   search -> .git   (committed symlink, stays inside the opened root)
entire graph search --repo REPO --head --query q --cache-dir REPO
  -> REPO/.git/search-snapshot-v12/<sha256>.json.gz
```

The destination filename is a digest, so this creates directories and files rather than
overwriting a chosen victim, and `os.Rename` already replaced a symlink at the artifact name
instead of following it. The directory components were the whole of the hole.

## The same defect is also a permanent cache miss

`cacheEntry.open` reads through `os.OpenRoot(cacheDir)`, which refuses exactly the components
the write followed — `TestCacheEntryReadRejectsSymlinkEscape` pins that. So a symlinked
descendant produced an entry that was **written on every run and read on none**. Measured on
the same repository and query, artifact mtime after two runs:

```
plain cache directory:      1787885558, 1787885558   (hit, not rewritten)
symlinked family component: 1787885508, 1787885561   (miss, rewritten every run)
```

That is why the refusal costs nothing that works today: every configuration it now rejects has
never produced a cache hit.

## The fix

`cacheEntry.write` replaces both bodies. The cache root stays caller-named and is still
resolved as given, so a symlinked cache *directory* — the deployment that puts the cache on
another volume, in a shared location, or outside a container's writable layer — keeps working
on both sides. Below the root, each component is created and then `Lstat`-checked before being
descended into through its own opened handle, and a symlink there is refused.

`os.Root` alone is not enough for the second half, for the reason `outputpath.go` records: it
stops a link leaving the root but follows one that stays inside it, and with the cache
directory at a checkout root, `.git` is inside it. The `Lstat` check is not an exact-case
comparison, so a case-insensitive filesystem cannot answer it with a differently-spelled link.

The temporary file moves with it: a `crypto/rand` name opened `O_CREATE|O_EXCL` inside the
checked directory handle, keeping the `.snapshot-*.json.gz` / `.records-*.json.gz` shape that
cleanup globs match, and the install is `Rename` within that same handle.

Query-time caching is best effort and those call sites discard the error, so a refusal is a
cache miss there. `index`'s explicit persist reports it:

```
persist preindex snapshot: cache directory component "search" is a symlink
```

## Tests

`internal/sem/cache_write_confinement_test.go`, all five refusal assertions verified to fail
with the production change reverted and the tests kept:

- family component symlinked out of the cache directory (both families)
- family component symlinked to `.git`, staying inside the opened root (both families)
- version component symlinked out

plus three that pin what must not change: a symlinked cache root still round-trips at mode
0600, a symlink at the artifact name is replaced rather than written through, and a successful
write leaves only the artifact.

## Two existing tests changed, and why

`TestCacheWritesTolerateSymlinkedCacheDirectories` pinned the old behaviour, calling a symlinked
family subdirectory "a supported operator layout (a larger volume, a shared cache, an escape from
a container's writable layer)" whose artifact "must still be written **and read back through it**".

The read-back half was never true, and nothing asserted it. Every one of those three motivations
needs a link that LEAVES the cache directory, and that is exactly what the reader refuses.
Measured on unmodified `main`, with `cache/search -> ../backing`:

```
write:     ok, artifact lands in backing/v1/<key>.json.gz
read back: openat search/v1/<key>.json.gz: path escapes from parent
```

The only family link that does round-trip is one pointing back inside the cache directory, which
cannot reach another volume. So the test is replaced by
`TestCacheWritesRefuseSymlinkedFamilyDirectories`, which pins both halves: an artifact placed
behind the link by hand is still unreachable through it, and the write no longer pretends
otherwise.

`TestSearchCacheLoadersRejectSymlinkEscape`'s last block asserted that `preindex` persists beneath
such a cache directory. It now asserts the refusal and that the message names the component: an
entry the durability read cannot see is not a durable artifact, so reporting it is the honest
outcome for a verb whose whole job is to promise one.

## Verification

`go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, `gofmt -l` clean, and `go test ./...` green across every package
(`internal/sem` 863s, `internal/cli` 153s under load).

CI is green on all three platforms, including the Windows mode-bits fix in the second commit.

Correction to an earlier claim in this description: one test was skipped in the local run above,
`TestWriteOutputFileDoesNotFollowALinkSwappedInAfterTheCheck`
(`internal/cli/outputpath_test.go`), because it blew a 4-minute timeout locally — including on an
unmodified `origin/main` worktree, which is why it was reported as unrelated to this change. CI has
since run it on all three platforms and it passes, so it was local starvation (the test spins until
it wins a race, and this machine was running several suites concurrently), not a non-termination.
Nothing is outstanding against it.

Every claim above was reproduced by driving the built binary against a scratch repository with
committed `mode 120000` entries, before and after, for both cache families.

### 1. `internal/sem/cache_entry.go:183` — Windows junctions are `ModeIrregular`, not `ModeSymlink` — **VALID**

The guard tested `info.Mode()&fs.ModeSymlink != 0`. That is the right test on Unix and the wrong one on Windows: a symlink is reported as `ModeSymlink`, but a directory junction or mount point is reported as `ModeIrregular`. A junction planted at the `family` or `version` component therefore passed the check and was then descended into and followed — exactly the redirect this guard exists to refuse.

This repository already had the correct predicate, with five production call sites:

```
internal/sem/path_redirect_windows.go:12   return info.Mode()&(os.ModeSymlink|os.ModeIrregular) != 0
internal/sem/path_redirect_other.go:8      return info.Mode()&os.ModeSymlink != 0
```
callers: `provider.go:11777`, `provider.go:13200`, `provider.go:15057`, `sweep_open_other.go:68`, `metadata_tree_entry_windows.go:37` — all in `package sem`, so it is a drop-in here.

**Fix:** `openCacheComponent` now calls `cacheComponentRedirectError`, which tests `pathMayRedirect(info)`. The message keeps the substring `is a symlink` that `search_cache_test.go:161` matches on, and names the mode it found.

---

### 2. `internal/sem/cache_entry.go:194` — `rand.Text()` terminates the process — **VALID** (and stronger than described)

Verified in the toolchain's own source. `crypto/rand.Text` calls `Read`, and `crypto/rand/rand.go`:

```go
// Read calls [io.ReadFull] on [Reader] and crashes the program irrecoverably if
// an error is returned. …
	if err != nil {
		fatal("crypto/rand: failed to read random data (see https://go.dev/issue/66821): " + err.Error())
		panic("unreachable") // To be sure.
	}
```

`fatal` is `runtime.fatal` via `go:linkname`, reaching `fatalthrow` — the runtime's unrecoverable throw. So it is **not** a panic a caller can `recover`; it is a hard process kill. Tearing down a whole index run because a temporary cache file could not be named is the wrong failure mode for a best-effort write whose errors every caller already discards.

For contrast, `os.CreateTemp` never has this exposure: `$GOROOT/src/os/tempfile.go` names its files from `runtime.rand()`, an infallible non-cryptographic source. This code wants the CSPRNG for the O_EXCL race guard, so the answer is not to drop to a weaker source but to read it through an interface that reports.

**Fix:** `cacheTempNameSuffix(source io.Reader)` reads 16 bytes with `io.ReadFull(rand.Reader, …)` and hex-encodes them — same CSPRNG, error returned instead of a process kill.

---

### 3. `internal/sem/cache_entry.go:186` — TOCTOU between `Lstat` and `OpenRoot` — **REFUTED**

The race window is real; the consequence it implies is not. `os.Root` enforces confinement inside the syscall, independently of any `Lstat` the caller did first, so winning the race cannot make the write escape the cache root.

Standalone probe against the same toolchain (`go1.26.0 darwin/arm64`), exercising every operation this code performs through the returned handle:

```
A OpenRoot(link -> ../outside RELATIVE): ERROR: openat link: path escapes from parent
B OpenRoot(link -> ABS outside path):    ERROR: openat link: path escapes from parent
C OpenRoot(link -> sibling INSIDE root): OK (no error)
C sub.Open(in.txt):                      SUCCESS, read "INSIDE-BYTES"
D OpenFile(link/x -> ../outside REL):    ERROR: openat link/x: path escapes from parent
E OpenFile(link/y -> ABS outside path):  ERROR: openat link/y: path escapes from parent
F Rename(src.txt -> link/z.txt):         ERROR: renameat src.txt link/z.txt: path escapes from parent
```

`go doc os.Root`:

> Methods on Root will follow symbolic links, but symbolic links may not reference a location outside the root. Symbolic links must not be absolute.

So the worst a won race can do is case C: redirect the write to **another location inside the same cache root**, which `os.Root` permits by design. That is not a privilege gain — whoever can plant the symlink at that component already has write access to the cache directory and can simply write the target path directly. The `Lstat` is a nicer error ahead of an enforcement that happens anyway, not the boundary itself.

No change made. Closing the window would mean re-deriving through a handle `os.Root` already re-derives, for an outcome `os.Root` already guarantees.

(The one documented exception is `GOOS=js`, where `os.Root` states it *is* vulnerable to symlink TOCTOU and cannot ensure confinement. This tool is not built for js/wasm.)

---

### Tests

In `internal/sem/cache_write_confinement_test.go`:

- `TestCacheComponentRedirectErrorHonoursEveryRedirectingMode` — table over `ModeDir`, `ModeSymlink`, `ModeIrregular|ModeDir`, presented through a stub `os.FileInfo`. The `ModeIrregular` row expects a refusal only where `runtime.GOOS == "windows"`, and expects **no** refusal elsewhere, so it also pins that ordinary irregular entries are not broken on platforms with no reparse points. A junction cannot be created in-process (privileges + `mklink`), and the guard either honours the bit or does not.
- `TestCacheTempNameSuffixReportsRandomnessFailure` — an erroring source and a short source must both be reported.
- `TestCacheTempNameSuffixIsUnpredictable` — 64 distinct 32-character lowercase-hex draws.
- `TestCreateRootTempNamesTheFileFromTheReportedRandomSource` — the call-site guard; the hex shape is what distinguishes it from `rand.Text`.

| mutation | result |
|---|---|

| `createRootTemp` reverted to `rand.Text()` | **caught** — `temporary cache file named ".REDACTED.json.gz", want .snapshot-<32 hexadecimal>.json.gz` |

## The write

`writeSearchSnapshot` and `writeProviderRecords` installed their artifact with
`os.MkdirAll` + `os.CreateTemp` + `os.Rename` on the joined path. `os.MkdirAll` follows a
symlinked directory component, so `<cache>/search` or `<cache>/search/search-snapshot-v12`
decided where the artifact actually landed.

`cacheEntry.writePath`'s comment argued that this was safe because "the cache directory is
caller-owned" and "anyone who can plant a symlink inside the cache directory can write the
artifact directly". Both halves hold only while the cache directory is somewhere the caller
owns. `--cache-dir` and `ENTIRE_PLUGIN_DATA_DIR` take any path, including one inside the
scanned checkout, and then the planter is the repository — the same reasoning
`internal/cli/outputpath.go` already applies to `index --report` when the caller names a path
inside the checkout.

Reproduced against a scratch repository holding two committed `mode 120000` entries:

```
# .egcache/search -> /outside   (committed symlink, escapes the cache directory)
entire graph search --repo REPO --head --query q --cache-dir REPO/.egcache
  -> /outside/search-snapshot-v12/<sha256>.json.gz

# .git-linked family, cache directory at the checkout root
#   search -> .git   (committed symlink, stays inside the opened root)
entire graph search --repo REPO --head --query q --cache-dir REPO
  -> REPO/.git/search-snapshot-v12/<sha256>.json.gz
```

The destination filename is a digest, so this creates directories and files rather than
overwriting a chosen victim, and `os.Rename` already replaced a symlink at the artifact name
instead of following it. The directory components were the whole of the hole.

## The same defect is also a permanent cache miss

`cacheEntry.open` reads through `os.OpenRoot(cacheDir)`, which refuses exactly the components
the write followed — `TestCacheEntryReadRejectsSymlinkEscape` pins that. So a symlinked
descendant produced an entry that was **written on every run and read on none**. Measured on
the same repository and query, artifact mtime after two runs:

```
plain cache directory:      1787885558, 1787885558   (hit, not rewritten)
symlinked family component: 1787885508, 1787885561   (miss, rewritten every run)
```

That is why the refusal costs nothing that works today: every configuration it now rejects has
never produced a cache hit.

## The fix

`cacheEntry.write` replaces both bodies. The cache root stays caller-named and is still
resolved as given, so a symlinked cache *directory* — the deployment that puts the cache on
another volume, in a shared location, or outside a container's writable layer — keeps working
on both sides. Below the root, each component is created and then `Lstat`-checked before being
descended into through its own opened handle, and a symlink there is refused.

`os.Root` alone is not enough for the second half, for the reason `outputpath.go` records: it
stops a link leaving the root but follows one that stays inside it, and with the cache
directory at a checkout root, `.git` is inside it. The `Lstat` check is not an exact-case
comparison, so a case-insensitive filesystem cannot answer it with a differently-spelled link.

The temporary file moves with it: a `crypto/rand` name opened `O_CREATE|O_EXCL` inside the
checked directory handle, keeping the `.snapshot-*.json.gz` / `.records-*.json.gz` shape that
cleanup globs match, and the install is `Rename` within that same handle.

Query-time caching is best effort and those call sites discard the error, so a refusal is a
cache miss there. `index`'s explicit persist reports it:

```
persist preindex snapshot: cache directory component "search" is a symlink
```

## Tests

`internal/sem/cache_write_confinement_test.go`, all five refusal assertions verified to fail
with the production change reverted and the tests kept:

- family component symlinked out of the cache directory (both families)
- family component symlinked to `.git`, staying inside the opened root (both families)
- version component symlinked out

plus three that pin what must not change: a symlinked cache root still round-trips at mode
0600, a symlink at the artifact name is replaced rather than written through, and a successful
write leaves only the artifact.

## Two existing tests changed, and why

`TestCacheWritesTolerateSymlinkedCacheDirectories` pinned the old behaviour, calling a symlinked
family subdirectory "a supported operator layout (a larger volume, a shared cache, an escape from
a container's writable layer)" whose artifact "must still be written **and read back through it**".

The read-back half was never true, and nothing asserted it. Every one of those three motivations
needs a link that LEAVES the cache directory, and that is exactly what the reader refuses.
Measured on unmodified `main`, with `cache/search -> ../backing`:

```
write:     ok, artifact lands in backing/v1/<key>.json.gz
read back: openat search/v1/<key>.json.gz: path escapes from parent
```

The only family link that does round-trip is one pointing back inside the cache directory, which
cannot reach another volume. So the test is replaced by
`TestCacheWritesRefuseSymlinkedFamilyDirectories`, which pins both halves: an artifact placed
behind the link by hand is still unreachable through it, and the write no longer pretends
otherwise.

`TestSearchCacheLoadersRejectSymlinkEscape`'s last block asserted that `preindex` persists beneath
such a cache directory. It now asserts the refusal and that the message names the component: an
entry the durability read cannot see is not a durable artifact, so reporting it is the honest
outcome for a verb whose whole job is to promise one.

## Verification

`go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, `gofmt -l` clean, and `go test ./...` green across every package
(`internal/sem` 863s, `internal/cli` 153s under load).

CI is green on all three platforms, including the Windows mode-bits fix in the second commit.

Correction to an earlier claim in this description: one test was skipped in the local run above,
`TestWriteOutputFileDoesNotFollowALinkSwappedInAfterTheCheck`
(`internal/cli/outputpath_test.go`), because it blew a 4-minute timeout locally — including on an
unmodified `origin/main` worktree, which is why it was reported as unrelated to this change. CI has
since run it on all three platforms and it passes, so it was local starvation (the test spins until
it wins a race, and this machine was running several suites concurrently), not a non-termination.
Nothing is outstanding against it.

Every claim above was reproduced by driving the built binary against a scratch repository with
committed `mode 120000` entries, before and after, for both cache families.

A junction planted at the `family` or `version` component therefore passed the check and was then descended into and followed — exactly the redirect this guard exists to refuse.

This repository already had the correct predicate, with five production call sites:

```
internal/sem/path_redirect_windows.go:12   return info.Mode()&(os.ModeSymlink|os.ModeIrregular) != 0
internal/sem/path_redirect_other.go:8      return info.Mode()&os.ModeSymlink != 0
```
callers: `provider.go:11777`, `provider.go:13200`, `provider.go:15057`, `sweep_open_other.go:68`, `metadata_tree_entry_windows.go:37` — all in `package sem`, so it is a drop-in here.

**Fix:** `openCacheComponent` now calls `cacheComponentRedirectError`, which tests `pathMayRedirect(info)`. The message keeps the substring `is a symlink` that `search_cache_test.go:161` matches on, and names the mode it found.

---

### 2. `internal/sem/cache_entry.go:194` — `rand.Text()` terminates the process — **VALID** (and stronger than described)

Verified in the toolchain's own source. `crypto/rand.Text` calls `Read`, and `crypto/rand/rand.go`:

```go
// Read calls [io.ReadFull] on [Reader] and crashes the program irrecoverably if
// an error is returned. …
	if err != nil {
		fatal("crypto/rand: failed to read random data (see https://go.dev/issue/66821): " + err.Error())
		panic("unreachable") // To be sure.
	}
```

`fatal` is `runtime.fatal` via `go:linkname`, reaching `fatalthrow` — the runtime's unrecoverable throw. So it is **not** a panic a caller can `recover`; it is a hard process kill. Tearing down a whole index run because a temporary cache file could not be named is the wrong failure mode for a best-effort write whose errors every caller already discards.

For contrast, `os.CreateTemp` never has this exposure: `$GOROOT/src/os/tempfile.go` names its files from `runtime.rand()`, an infallible non-cryptographic source. This code wants the CSPRNG for the O_EXCL race guard, so the answer is not to drop to a weaker source but to read it through an interface that reports.

**Fix:** `cacheTempNameSuffix(source io.Reader)` reads 16 bytes with `io.ReadFull(rand.Reader, …)` and hex-encodes them — same CSPRNG, error returned instead of a process kill.

---

### 3. `internal/sem/cache_entry.go:186` — TOCTOU between `Lstat` and `OpenRoot` — **REFUTED**

The race window is real; the consequence it implies is not. `os.Root` enforces confinement inside the syscall, independently of any `Lstat` the caller did first, so winning the race cannot make the write escape the cache root.

Standalone probe against the same toolchain (`go1.26.0 darwin/arm64`), exercising every operation this code performs through the returned handle:

```
A OpenRoot(link -> ../outside RELATIVE): ERROR: openat link: path escapes from parent
B OpenRoot(link -> ABS outside path):    ERROR: openat link: path escapes from parent
C OpenRoot(link -> sibling INSIDE root): OK (no error)
C sub.Open(in.txt):                      SUCCESS, read "INSIDE-BYTES"
D OpenFile(link/x -> ../outside REL):    ERROR: openat link/x: path escapes from parent
E OpenFile(link/y -> ABS outside path):  ERROR: openat link/y: path escapes from parent
F Rename(src.txt -> link/z.txt):         ERROR: renameat src.txt link/z.txt: path escapes from parent
```

`go doc os.Root`:

> Methods on Root will follow symbolic links, but symbolic links may not reference a location outside the root. Symbolic links must not be absolute.

So the worst a won race can do is case C: redirect the write to **another location inside the same cache root**, which `os.Root` permits by design. That is not a privilege gain — whoever can plant the symlink at that component already has write access to the cache directory and can simply write the target path directly. The `Lstat` is a nicer error ahead of an enforcement that happens anyway, not the boundary itself.

No change made. Closing the window would mean re-deriving through a handle `os.Root` already re-derives, for an outcome `os.Root` already guarantees.

(The one documented exception is `GOOS=js`, where `os.Root` states it *is* vulnerable to symlink TOCTOU and cannot ensure confinement. This tool is not built for js/wasm.)

---

### Tests

In `internal/sem/cache_write_confinement_test.go`:

- `TestCacheComponentRedirectErrorHonoursEveryRedirectingMode` — table over `ModeDir`, `ModeSymlink`, `ModeIrregular|ModeDir`, presented through a stub `os.FileInfo`. The `ModeIrregular` row expects a refusal only where `runtime.GOOS == "windows"`, and expects **no** refusal elsewhere, so it also pins that ordinary irregular entries are not broken on platforms with no reparse points. A junction cannot be created in-process (privileges + `mklink`), and the guard either honours the bit or does not.
- `TestCacheTempNameSuffixReportsRandomnessFailure` — an erroring source and a short source must both be reported.
- `TestCacheTempNameSuffixIsUnpredictable` — 64 distinct 32-character lowercase-hex draws.
- `TestCreateRootTempNamesTheFileFromTheReportedRandomSource` — the call-site guard; the hex shape is what distinguishes it from `rand.Text`.

### Mutation verification

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| `cacheTempNameSuffix` swallows the read error (`_ = err`) | **caught** — `cacheTempNameSuffix error = <nil>, want it to report randomness source unavailable` |
| `createRootTemp` reverted to `rand.Text()` | **caught** — `temporary cache file named ".REDACTED.json.gz", want .snapshot-<32 hexadecimal>.json.gz` |
| guard forced to accept everything (`if true \|\| !pathMayRedirect(info)`) | **caught** — symlink row fails |
| non-Windows `pathMayRedirect` widened to include `ModeIrregular` | **caught** — `mode d?--------- was refused on darwin` |
| guard reverted to `ModeSymlink`-only | **not caught on darwin, as expected** — the two predicates are identical on this platform by construction. That row discriminates only where the modes differ, i.e. on the `windows-latest` leg of `test.yml`. Stated rather than papered over. |

Each mutation was `grep`-confirmed applied before running, and the restore `grep`-confirmed after. `go test ./internal/sem -run 'Cache|Snapshot|Symlink|Confin'` passes; `go vet` and `gofmt -l` clean.

## The write

`writeSearchSnapshot` and `writeProviderRecords` installed their artifact with
`os.MkdirAll` + `os.CreateTemp` + `os.Rename` on the joined path. `os.MkdirAll` follows a
symlinked directory component, so `<cache>/search` or `<cache>/search/search-snapshot-v12`
decided where the artifact actually landed.

`cacheEntry.writePath`'s comment argued that this was safe because "the cache directory is
caller-owned" and "anyone who can plant a symlink inside the cache directory can write the
artifact directly". Both halves hold only while the cache directory is somewhere the caller
owns. `--cache-dir` and `ENTIRE_PLUGIN_DATA_DIR` take any path, including one inside the
scanned checkout, and then the planter is the repository — the same reasoning
`internal/cli/outputpath.go` already applies to `index --report` when the caller names a path
inside the checkout.

Reproduced against a scratch repository holding two committed `mode 120000` entries:

```
# .egcache/search -> /outside   (committed symlink, escapes the cache directory)
entire graph search --repo REPO --head --query q --cache-dir REPO/.egcache
  -> /outside/search-snapshot-v12/<sha256>.json.gz

# .git-linked family, cache directory at the checkout root
#   search -> .git   (committed symlink, stays inside the opened root)
entire graph search --repo REPO --head --query q --cache-dir REPO
  -> REPO/.git/search-snapshot-v12/<sha256>.json.gz
```

The destination filename is a digest, so this creates directories and files rather than
overwriting a chosen victim, and `os.Rename` already replaced a symlink at the artifact name
instead of following it. The directory components were the whole of the hole.

## The same defect is also a permanent cache miss

`cacheEntry.open` reads through `os.OpenRoot(cacheDir)`, which refuses exactly the components
the write followed — `TestCacheEntryReadRejectsSymlinkEscape` pins that. So a symlinked
descendant produced an entry that was **written on every run and read on none**. Measured on
the same repository and query, artifact mtime after two runs:

```
plain cache directory:      1787885558, 1787885558   (hit, not rewritten)
symlinked family component: 1787885508, 1787885561   (miss, rewritten every run)
```

That is why the refusal costs nothing that works today: every configuration it now rejects has
never produced a cache hit.

## The fix

`cacheEntry.write` replaces both bodies. The cache root stays caller-named and is still
resolved as given, so a symlinked cache *directory* — the deployment that puts the cache on
another volume, in a shared location, or outside a container's writable layer — keeps working
on both sides. Below the root, each component is created and then `Lstat`-checked before being
descended into through its own opened handle, and a symlink there is refused.

`os.Root` alone is not enough for the second half, for the reason `outputpath.go` records: it
stops a link leaving the root but follows one that stays inside it, and with the cache
directory at a checkout root, `.git` is inside it. The `Lstat` check is not an exact-case
comparison, so a case-insensitive filesystem cannot answer it with a differently-spelled link.

The temporary file moves with it: a `crypto/rand` name opened `O_CREATE|O_EXCL` inside the
checked directory handle, keeping the `.snapshot-*.json.gz` / `.records-*.json.gz` shape that
cleanup globs match, and the install is `Rename` within that same handle.

Query-time caching is best effort and those call sites discard the error, so a refusal is a
cache miss there. `index`'s explicit persist reports it:

```
persist preindex snapshot: cache directory component "search" is a symlink
```

## Tests

`internal/sem/cache_write_confinement_test.go`, all five refusal assertions verified to fail
with the production change reverted and the tests kept:

- family component symlinked out of the cache directory (both families)
- family component symlinked to `.git`, staying inside the opened root (both families)
- version component symlinked out

plus three that pin what must not change: a symlinked cache root still round-trips at mode
0600, a symlink at the artifact name is replaced rather than written through, and a successful
write leaves only the artifact.

## Two existing tests changed, and why

`TestCacheWritesTolerateSymlinkedCacheDirectories` pinned the old behaviour, calling a symlinked
family subdirectory "a supported operator layout (a larger volume, a shared cache, an escape from
a container's writable layer)" whose artifact "must still be written **and read back through it**".

The read-back half was never true, and nothing asserted it. Every one of those three motivations
needs a link that LEAVES the cache directory, and that is exactly what the reader refuses.
Measured on unmodified `main`, with `cache/search -> ../backing`:

```
write:     ok, artifact lands in backing/v1/<key>.json.gz
read back: openat search/v1/<key>.json.gz: path escapes from parent
```

The only family link that does round-trip is one pointing back inside the cache directory, which
cannot reach another volume. So the test is replaced by
`TestCacheWritesRefuseSymlinkedFamilyDirectories`, which pins both halves: an artifact placed
behind the link by hand is still unreachable through it, and the write no longer pretends
otherwise.

`TestSearchCacheLoadersRejectSymlinkEscape`'s last block asserted that `preindex` persists beneath
such a cache directory. It now asserts the refusal and that the message names the component: an
entry the durability read cannot see is not a durable artifact, so reporting it is the honest
outcome for a verb whose whole job is to promise one.

## Verification

`go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, `gofmt -l` clean, and `go test ./...` green across every package
(`internal/sem` 863s, `internal/cli` 153s under load).

CI is green on all three platforms, including the Windows mode-bits fix in the second commit.

Correction to an earlier claim in this description: one test was skipped in the local run above,
`TestWriteOutputFileDoesNotFollowALinkSwappedInAfterTheCheck`
(`internal/cli/outputpath_test.go`), because it blew a 4-minute timeout locally — including on an
unmodified `origin/main` worktree, which is why it was reported as unrelated to this change. CI has
since run it on all three platforms and it passes, so it was local starvation (the test spins until
it wins a race, and this machine was running several suites concurrently), not a non-termination.
Nothing is outstanding against it.

Every claim above was reproduced by driving the built binary against a scratch repository with
committed `mode 120000` entries, before and after, for both cache families.

So the worst a won race can do is case C: redirect the write to **another location inside the same cache root**, which `os.Root` permits by design. No change made. Closing the window would mean re-deriving through a handle `os.Root` already re-derives, for an outcome `os.Root` already guarantees.

(The one documented exception is `GOOS=js`, where `os.Root` states it *is* vulnerable to symlink TOCTOU and cannot ensure confinement. This tool is not built for js/wasm.)

In `internal/sem/cache_write_confinement_test.go`:

# Trust and security

This page states what Entire Graph reads, writes, executes, and sends over the
network, scoped precisely enough to be checked. Statements match the 0.4.0
release target and the implementation under `internal/`.

## Network

The built-in analyzer is local-only. During analysis it does not fetch remote
code, download grammars or models, call hosted APIs, resolve embeddings, or
send telemetry. Tree-sitter grammars are compiled into the binary. The
benchmark harness's clone phase and `entire plugin install graph` are the
networked operations, and both are explicit: one is a development tool, the
other is installation.

## What it reads

- Repository content: the working tree (default for interactive queries) or
  committed objects via `git` (for `--head`, bulk streams, and `diff`/
  `commit`).
- Bounded local Git history, for co-change relations (`FILE_CHANGES_WITH`) and
  change analysis. History never leaves the machine.
- Structural Git metadata needed by those subprocesses. Before Git starts, the
  provider walks the resolved administrative/common directories and recursive
  alternate object stores from held handles, with fixed entry and
  resolver-relative-path bounds, and rejects mount points, off-volume redirects,
  and special files.
  Git's own fsmonitor daemon socket is permitted because every provider Git
  subprocess explicitly disables `core.fsmonitor`. Before those subprocesses
  start, inherited global and system Git configuration is disabled. Protected
  command-scope `safe.directory` entries authorize only the selected command
  directory and its ancestors (the exact repository-discovery candidates),
  never the unrestricted `*` value, so explicitly selected shared checkouts
  remain usable without trusting unrelated repositories. The bounded
  repository-metadata preflight rejects active repository-local
  `[include]` and `[includeIf]` sections, including in an enabled
  `config.worktree`. Repository-local configuration remains available for
  structural settings Git needs; active `core.worktree` paths are checked by
  the same rooted preflight. Active partial-clone/promisor configuration is
  refused because supported Git versions before 2.45 can inspect a local or UNC
  promisor URL before enforcing the transport deny-list. At command scope the
  provider sets
  `core.fsmonitor=false`, `log.showSignature=false`, `log.mailmap=false`,
  `submodule.recurse=false`, and empty values for `core.excludesFile` and
  `core.attributesFile`; `diff.orderFile` is pinned to the platform null device.
  Configuration-derived external ignore, attribute, mailmap, and diff-order
  files are therefore not read or honored, and grep does not enter nested
  submodule worktrees. Machine-readable grep calls explicitly disable configured
  line numbers, columns, color, and full-name rewriting. Working-tree snapshot
  caching stays disabled instead of asking Git's conversion-aware status
  machinery to run repository-configured clean or process filters. Remaining
  configuration-derived structural limitations, including relocated ref storage,
  are recorded in `docs/parking-lot.md`. Adjacent setup helpers reuse a
  repository-bound validation receipt only within the current operation;
  validation results are not cached globally or persisted.
- Before Git recursively enumerates untracked worktree content, a bounded
  held-root preflight walks the complete directory tree without resolving a
  nested case-insensitive `.git` marker. A nested marker selects the bounded
  filesystem fallback only after the preflight finishes checking every other
  directory. Unreadable local subtrees retain the fallback's warned omission,
  while the preflight continues across every other reachable directory. A
  traversable redirect, mount boundary, cancellation, or traversal ceiling
  fails closed. Every earlier Git failure also passes through this safety gate
  before the filesystem fallback begins. Under Go's legacy Windows reparse-mode
  compatibility, mount points surface as symlinks instead; both filesystem
  fallbacks apply their no-follow rule before considering a directory entry.
  This prevents an untracked gitfile from making Git resolve a UNC or off-volume
  target before the post-listing Git-directory excluder can observe it.
- `stats` applies the same worktree safety gate before sampling on-disk file
  sizes. Transcript-derived top-hit paths are confined beneath the selected
  repository and measured with a final-component no-follow lookup; an unsafe
  worktree contributes no filesystem-size estimate.
- Repository-controlled Git ignore policy, including nested `.gitignore` files,
  `.git/info/exclude`, and per-worktree excludes, plus `.graphignore` and any
  `--ignore-file`/`--include-file` the caller passes.
  Caller-supplied ignore inputs are bounded to 1 MiB per file and 64 KiB per rule
  line. One listing retains at most 16,384 parsed external rules and observes at
  most 512 nested `.gitignore` files. A limit refusal is reported instead of
  truncating the policy and silently changing the indexed corpus. Nested
  worktree ignore files are confined to the repository and are not followed
  through a symlink that escapes it. When Git cannot enumerate a worktree, the
  bounded filesystem fallback applies the ignore files it can observe and emits
  `W_GIT_WORKTREE_FALLBACK`; Git-only policy may be unavailable, so the warning
  explicitly reports that excluded files can be present. Configuration-derived
  `core.excludesFile` is outside the effective policy in both the Git and
  fallback paths. The fallback's ignored-tree `.git`-pointer sweep stays beneath
  a held repository root and refuses redirects or mount points (including
  same-filesystem bind mounts on Linux); a refused directory is disclosed as
  `W_GITDIR_SWEEP_UNREADABLE_DIRECTORY`.
- Inherited repository-selection, attribute-source, and pathspec-control
  variables, every `GIT_TRACE*` output target, and Git for Windows'
  `GIT_REDIRECT_*` standard-stream targets are removed from production Git
  subprocesses. `GIT_TEXTDOMAINDIR` is removed too because Git probes it during
  startup. Those inherited values therefore cannot open an arbitrary path or
  socket (including a Windows UNC target) or replace explicit machine-command
  path semantics. When `GIT_CEILING_DIRECTORIES` is present during implicit
  discovery, the CLI applies usable absolute entries in-process. Entries before
  Git's first empty-list marker are canonicalized with a same-volume guarded
  walk; subsequent entries stay lexical as Git specifies. The CLI never gives
  Git the raw list, whose canonicalization could itself probe an off-volume or
  UNC path. If a pre-marker entry cannot be resolved without such a probe,
  implicit discovery fails closed. All selected-repository subprocesses
  discard it.
- For `stats` only: local coding-agent session transcripts
  (`~/.claude/projects/<path-slug>/*.jsonl`, or `--sessions-dir`/
  `--transcript` overrides). This is Claude Code's transcript layout; the
  report is read-only and local. No other command reads transcripts.

### Credential-store path exclusions

A built-in exclude list keeps credential stores out of the provider's
working-tree and committed-tree source corpora. Within those corpora, unless a
caller deliberately re-admits one, a denied path is not parsed as source,
indexed, written to graph/search caches, returned in graph or search results, or
quoted in search context blocks.

This is a corpus and output boundary, not a promise that no local process reads
the underlying file or Git blob. Git-backed search acceleration can scan
tracked or committed blobs before credential-store path rules are applied to
its matches; denied matches are discarded before Entire Graph's content reader,
source parser, caches or responses. The `diff`, `analyze`, `commit` and
`checkpoint` families analyze requested Git ranges rather than the graph/search
corpus, so they can read credential-store paths and report content-derived
metadata about them. Those built-in operations remain local under the provider's
no-egress contract. `verify` runs caller-supplied commands with the caller's
privileges and is outside this exclusion boundary.

The list covers `.env` and its `.env.<environment>` variants, `.envrc`,
`.npmrc`, `.netrc`/`_netrc`, `.pgpass`, `.htpasswd`, `.pypirc`, `.dockercfg`,
`.boto`, `.git-credentials`, Docker's `.docker/config.json`, Kubernetes'
`.kube/config`, Terraform's `credentials.tfrc.json`, Google Cloud's
`application_default_credentials.json`, SSH private keys (`id_rsa`, `id_dsa`,
`id_ecdsa`, `id_ed25519`),
`credentials`/`credentials.{json,yml,yaml,ini,toml}`,
`secrets.{json,yml,yaml,ini,toml}`, key material and encrypted stores by suffix
(`.pem`, `.key`, `.pfx`, `.p12`, `.pkcs12`, `.jks`, `.keystore`, `.truststore`,
`.ppk`, `.kdbx`, `.asc`, `.gpg`), and files ending in `.yaml`, `.yml`, `.json`,
`.ini`, `.toml`, `.cfg`, `.conf`, `.properties`, `.txt` or `.enc` under a
directory segment named `secrets/` or `credentials/` at any depth. Matching is
case-insensitive. The Git, Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform, and Google Cloud
entries match at any depth and are file-only, so a same-named directory and its
descendants remain searchable.

Outside those file-only entries, matching retains Git-style path semantics. A
basename or suffix pattern can therefore match a directory segment; when it
does, that directory's descendants are excluded. For example, `*.key` also
excludes `pkg/client.key/**`. This behavior is intentional.

Classification is based on PATHS, not content: Entire Graph does not inspect a
file's bytes to decide whether an otherwise-unrecognized path contains a
secret. A credential store whose path gives no signal — `deploy/prod-values.yaml`
holding an inline API key — is not covered. Public halves (`.crt`, `.cer`,
`.pub`) are deliberately not excluded, and source code under
`internal/secrets/` or `pkg/credentials/` stays fully searchable.

The list is loaded after the repository's own exclude files, so a negation
inside the repository under analysis cannot switch it off, and before the
caller's `--ignore-file`/`--include-file`, so `--include-file` remains the way
to deliberately re-admit a path (a checked-in `.env.example` used as
configuration documentation, for example).

Because of that position the list only ever adds exclusions: it contains no
negation, so it cannot re-admit anything the repository itself excluded. The
bare `credentials` entry — the AWS CLI shape, `.aws/credentials` — is matched as
a FILENAME only for that reason: a directory named `credentials/` is neither
excluded by it nor re-admitted when the repository's own `.gitignore` or
`.graphignore` excludes it.

Both persistent caches (`index`/`search` snapshots and the streamed record
caches) key on a digest of the effective built-in rules, so a cache entry warmed
by a build with a different policy is not reachable — an entry written before
these rules existed misses instead of re-emitting the paths it named.

- Derivative caches, under `--cache-dir`, else `ENTIRE_PLUGIN_DATA_DIR`, else

  compressed snapshots rebuilt from repository state; deleting them costs a
  rebuild, nothing else. Queries never modify repository source files. The

- Inherited repository-selection, attribute-source, and pathspec-control
  variables, every `GIT_TRACE*` output target, and Git for Windows'
  `GIT_REDIRECT_*` standard-stream targets are removed from production Git
  subprocesses. `GIT_TEXTDOMAINDIR` is removed too because Git probes it during
  startup. Those inherited values therefore cannot open an arbitrary path or
  socket (including a Windows UNC target) or replace explicit machine-command
  path semantics. When `GIT_CEILING_DIRECTORIES` is present during implicit
  discovery, the CLI applies usable absolute entries in-process. Entries before
  Git's first empty-list marker are canonicalized with a same-volume guarded
  walk; subsequent entries stay lexical as Git specifies. The CLI never gives
  Git the raw list, whose canonicalization could itself probe an off-volume or
  UNC path. If a pre-marker entry cannot be resolved without such a probe,
  implicit discovery fails closed. All selected-repository subprocesses
  discard it.
- For `stats` only: local coding-agent session transcripts
  (`~/.claude/projects/<path-slug>/*.jsonl`, or `--sessions-dir`/
  `--transcript` overrides). This is Claude Code's transcript layout; the
  report is read-only and local. No other command reads transcripts.

### Credential-store path exclusions

A built-in exclude list keeps credential stores out of the provider's
working-tree and committed-tree source corpora. Within those corpora, unless a
caller deliberately re-admits one, a denied path is not parsed as source,
indexed, written to graph/search caches, returned in graph or search results, or
quoted in search context blocks.

This is a corpus and output boundary, not a promise that no local process reads
the underlying file or Git blob. Git-backed search acceleration can scan
tracked or committed blobs before credential-store path rules are applied to
its matches; denied matches are discarded before Entire Graph's content reader,
source parser, caches or responses. The `diff`, `analyze`, `commit` and
`checkpoint` families analyze requested Git ranges rather than the graph/search
corpus, so they can read credential-store paths and report content-derived
metadata about them. Those built-in operations remain local under the provider's
no-egress contract. `verify` runs caller-supplied commands with the caller's
privileges and is outside this exclusion boundary.

The list covers `.env` and its `.env.<environment>` variants, `.envrc`,
`.npmrc`, `.netrc`/`_netrc`, `.pgpass`, `.htpasswd`, `.pypirc`, `.dockercfg`,
`.boto`, `.git-credentials`, Docker's `.docker/config.json`, Kubernetes'
`.kube/config`, Terraform's `credentials.tfrc.json`, Google Cloud's
`application_default_credentials.json`, SSH private keys (`id_rsa`, `id_dsa`,
`id_ecdsa`, `id_ed25519`),
`credentials`/`credentials.{json,yml,yaml,ini,toml}`,
`secrets.{json,yml,yaml,ini,toml}`, key material and encrypted stores by suffix
(`.pem`, `.key`, `.pfx`, `.p12`, `.pkcs12`, `.jks`, `.keystore`, `.truststore`,
`.ppk`, `.kdbx`, `.asc`, `.gpg`), and files ending in `.yaml`, `.yml`, `.json`,
`.ini`, `.toml`, `.cfg`, `.conf`, `.properties`, `.txt` or `.enc` under a
directory segment named `secrets/` or `credentials/` at any depth. Matching is
case-insensitive. The Git, Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform, and Google Cloud
entries match at any depth and are file-only, so a same-named directory and its
descendants remain searchable.

Outside those file-only entries, matching retains Git-style path semantics. A
basename or suffix pattern can therefore match a directory segment; when it
does, that directory's descendants are excluded. For example, `*.key` also
excludes `pkg/client.key/**`. This behavior is intentional.

Classification is based on PATHS, not content: Entire Graph does not inspect a
file's bytes to decide whether an otherwise-unrecognized path contains a
secret. A credential store whose path gives no signal — `deploy/prod-values.yaml`
holding an inline API key — is not covered. Public halves (`.crt`, `.cer`,
`.pub`) are deliberately not excluded, and source code under
`internal/secrets/` or `pkg/credentials/` stays fully searchable.

The list is loaded after the repository's own exclude files, so a negation
inside the repository under analysis cannot switch it off, and before the
caller's `--ignore-file`/`--include-file`, so `--include-file` remains the way
to deliberately re-admit a path (a checked-in `.env.example` used as
configuration documentation, for example).

Because of that position the list only ever adds exclusions: it contains no
negation, so it cannot re-admit anything the repository itself excluded. The
bare `credentials` entry — the AWS CLI shape, `.aws/credentials` — is matched as
a FILENAME only for that reason: a directory named `credentials/` is neither
excluded by it nor re-admitted when the repository's own `.gitignore` or
`.graphignore` excludes it.

Both persistent caches (`index`/`search` snapshots and the streamed record
caches) key on a digest of the effective built-in rules, so a cache entry warmed
by a build with a different policy is not reachable — an entry written before
these rules existed misses instead of re-emitting the paths it named.

Message Type: FINAL_ANSWER
Task name: /root
Sender: /root/pr160_findings_audit
Payload:
The finding is technically valid under Go’s documented `os.Root` semantics.

- On Unix, descendant Roots hold directory FDs; renaming the directory does not invalidate the FD.
- On Windows, Go opens Root handles with `FILE_SHARE_DELETE`, so same-volume relocation is permitted.
- Go explicitly documents that when a rooted directory is moved, Root methods continue operating on the original directory in its new location.

Therefore, after `openCacheDirectory` validates `search/v1`, another process can move that directory outside `entry.root`; `createRootTemp` and `directory.Rename` then write through the still-valid handle at its new location.

There is no small, robust portable fix while retaining nested directories. Retaining the handle chain and rechecking identities before/after install only creates another race; temporary contents may already have been written outside, and an active mover can relocate between checks. Post-check cleanup is mitigation, not confinement.

Two defensible choices:

1. **Recommended: dismiss as outside the threat model**, and clarify the contract. The PR protects against repository-controlled static redirects and component substitution during opening—not a concurrently executing principal with namespace-mutation rights. Such a principal already has equivalent authority to move existing cache artifacts or write into the destination. Suggested dismissal reason:

   “`os.Root` intentionally follows an opened directory object across relocation. The cache threat model covers untrusted repository path entries, not a concurrent OS principal able to rename verified directories after opening; that principal already has equivalent filesystem authority. Portable Go cannot preserve a pathname-ancestry invariant against such relocation.”

   Add one sentence to the security docs stating that concurrent relocation of already-opened directories is outside the boundary.

2. **If active relocation must be defended against:** flatten cache artifacts so temporary and final files are direct children of the caller-selected cache root. Encode/hash `family/version/key` into one validated leaf filename. Then there is no movable descendant ancestor; root relocation remains explicitly part of the caller-selected root-object boundary. Test that cache entries have `filepath.Dir(relative) == "."`, a planted leaf symlink is replaced rather than followed, and legacy family/version redirects are never touched.

A deterministic reproduction for the current design is: open `search/v1`, move `search` to a same-volume directory outside the cache root, then create/rename through the held leaf Root and assert the artifact appears at the moved location. Do not resolve this with pre/post identity rechecks alone.

Message Type: MESSAGE
Task name: /root
Sender: /root/pr160_symlink_decision
Payload:

Two independent reviews agree this is not a normal TOCTOU patch: portable Go cannot pin a nested directory’s pathname against a concurrent process that is allowed to rename it. That leaves a real policy choice—scope the boundary to passive repository-controlled entries, or flatten the cache layout to remove movable descendant directories. I’m checking the last CI state before I put that choice to you.

That leaves a real policy choice—scope the boundary to passive repository-controlled entries, or flatten the cache layout to remove movable descendant directories. I’m checking the last CI state before I put that choice to you.

Message Type: FINAL_ANSWER
Task name: /root
Sender: /root/pr160_symlink_decision
Payload:
The finding is mechanically correct, but the stronger lexical-containment guarantee is impossible portably with the current hierarchical layout.

A held Unix directory can be renamed after verification; subsequent writes follow its inode. Revalidation only samples state and cannot close the final race. Portable mandatory directory-name locking does not exist.

Recommended resolution:

- Scope the guarantee to passive repository-controlled redirects and open-time identity mismatches.
- Document that writes subsequently use the verified directory capability and do not resist concurrent namespace relocation by another process with write authority.
- Dismiss this finding as out of threat model.

If active-renamer resistance is required, redesign the cache to store artifacts flat directly under the opened root, or prohibit cache roots inside checkouts. Repeated identity checks are not a complete fix.
